title.official: Recovery of goods and services tax

division.heading: Other Matters Related to Lawyers’ Charges and Litigation Costs

operative_text.controlling:
10.48(1)  Unless the Court otherwise orders, a party entitled to a
costs award is entitled to an additional amount on account of goods
and services tax
(a) on the fees portion of the costs award, and
(b) on those disbursements, if any, that are taxable supplies
under the Excise Tax Act (Canada).
(2)  Notwithstanding subrule (1), no additional amount on account
of goods and services tax is recoverable where the tax is refundable
or rebateable pursuant to the Excise Tax Act (Canada).

BOOK_A.title: Recovery of Goods and Services Tax
BOOK_A.commentary:
What is popularly called the goods and services tax, or "GST", is a tax levied under the federal
Excise Tax Act. (In many provinces, it is called the “harmonized sales tax” or “HST”. )
Rule 10.48 used to require an afﬁdavit saying that the GST is actually payable by the person
beneﬁtting from a costs award,⁵
but the court could waive that.⁶
That requirement has now been
taken out of the Rule, but a form replaces that. Form 44 (Writ of Enforcement) contains a warranty
that the recipient of party-party costs is not entitled to reimbursement of GST from anyone else.
That warranty has to be present and signed, to add GST to the costs.⁷
Most businesses are
entitled to that reimbursement from Revenue Canada, and so cannot add GST to party-party
costs.

This tax is in no sense compensation to a solicitor, who collects it merely as agent for the
government.¹
Where one party to the litigation is the federal government, it may be ordered to reimburse
any GST which the opposing side has paid on its litigation expenses.²
But if the party is a private
person, it may be presumed that he or she cannot pass GST on, and should be reimbursed for it.³
A municipality used to pay GST, but then got a rebate of about ½, and so could claim only the
net GST in costs.⁴

footnotes.text: Quite similar to previous R.605(9). It was ﬁrst enacted by Alta. Reg.38/03.
Quite similar to previous R.605(10). It was ﬁrst enacted by Alta. Reg.38/03, and amended later in 2003.

When enacted, the predecessor Rule removed the doubts expressed in a number of court decisions in the previous few years. GST was not added where there was doubt whether the payee of the costs would ultimately bear the burden of the GST: 574095 Alta. v. Brendanco Inv.2002 ABQB 487, 319 AR 383.
Horizon Res. Mgmt. v. Blaze Enr.2013 ABCA 139, 544 AR 239.

Especially where the person paying costs is not an ultimate consumer and is likely entitled to an input tax credit: Ekman v. Brooks (City) (#2) (M) 2022 ABQB 326, JCMH 1608 00432 (26 Oct ’21/5 May ’22) (¶ 9).
So a contractual cap on the solicitor’s compensation does not exclude G. S. T. : Morrison v. Rod Pantony P. C.2008 ABCA 145, 429 AR 259 (¶’s 22-3).
See the C. P. E. , Chapter 71, Part H.

Huet v. Lynch (#3), supra; Huet (V. A. H. ) v. Lynch 1998 ABCA 1020, 238 AR 201; Phillip v. Whitecourt Gen. Hosp. (#2) 2005 ABQB 174, 381 AR 234, affd 2006 ABCA 245, 397 AR 333, leave den (SCC 12 Apr ’07). But cf. Peter Pond Hldg. v. Shragge 2002 ABQB 746, 326 AR 44, revd other grds 2003 ABCA 290, 346 AR 135, leave den (SCC 22 Apr ’04), and Mar Automobile Hldg. v. Rawlusyk 2001 ABQB 516, 295 AR 152. Between pronouncement and entry of judgment, the trial judge added GST to the large amount which he had awarded, as by statute the plaintiff would have to pay that tax. He felt he had enough evidence: Klemke Mining Corp. v. Shell Can. (#2) 2007 ABQB 427, affd 2008 ABCA 257, 433 AR 172.
Peter Pond Hldg. v. Shragge, supra; Edm. Regl. Airports Authy. v. N. W. Geomatics (#2) 2003 ABQB 280, 332 AR 299.

The 'DIVISION 4 / SANCTIONS / Subdivision 1 / Penalty' headings (lines 7432-7435) belong to 10.49 and are printed after this note. Read against the official text: the rule text equals official 10.48 apart from the footnote markers and the amendment bracket (see the text note). (1) Related Provisions '10.31 (costs awards)' is a label for official 10.31 'Court-ordered costs award'. (2) 'Form 44 (Writ of Enforcement) contains a warranty that the recipient of party-party costs is not entitled to reimbursement of GST from anyone else' (lines 7402-7404) misnames the form: official Form 44 is 'Bill of Costs' ([Rule 10.35(1)], official line 23557), not a writ of enforcement, and it does contain a GST warranty (that the party entitled to the costs award is not entitled under the Excise Tax Act to a refund or rebate of GST paid); Book C also says 'Form 44 requires a warranty' but does not call it a writ. 'Rule 10.48 used to require an affidavit ... but the court could waive that' (fns 5-6) is history of the former rule; the official text of 10.48 today has no affidavit and no warranty requirement (the warranty is in Form 44); 'Most businesses are entitled to that reimbursement from Revenue Canada, and so cannot add GST' agrees with official 10.48(2) (no additional amount where the tax is refundable or rebateable). (3) Case-law statements in the note with their footnotes: 'This tax is in no sense compensation to a solicitor' (p.10-139 fn 1, Morrison v. Rod Pantony P. C. 2008 ABCA 145); the federal government reimbursing GST (fn 2 is a C. P. E. reference only); 'if the party is a private person, it may be presumed that he or she cannot pass GST on' (fn 3, Huet v. Lynch (#3), supra; Huet (V. A. H. ) v. Lynch 1998 ABCA 1020, 238 AR 201' prints the court label ABCA for the citation that the 10.29 note prints as 'Huet v. Lynch 1998 ABQB 1020, 238 AR 201' (line 2321; the same volume and page 238 AR 201, so one of the two labels is a misprint); fn 3 prints 'leave den (SCC 12 Apr ’07)' for Phillip v. Whitecourt Gen. Hosp. 2006 ABCA 245 (lines 7454-7455), the same year as lines 4360-4361 of the 10.31 note and unlike the '’97' of lines 3893 and 4249 (see the 10.31 flag); fn 4 'Peter Pond Hldg. v. BOOK_C.title: Recovery of goods and services tax
BOOK_C.division_heading: Division 3 – OTHER MATTERS RELATED TO LAWYERS’ CHARGES AND LITIGATION COSTS

commentary.text: This rule precludes recovery of GST in a costs award where the claiming party receives an input tax credit under the Excise Tax Act, because that is the sort of “reimbursement” contemplated by rule 10.48(2)(c) - and Form 44 requires a warranty to the effect that the GST will not be reimbursed by any other person. ConocoPhillips Canada Operations Ltd. v. 1835651 Alberta Ltd., [2020] A.J. No. 20, 2020 ABQB Rule 10.48 is prefaced by the words “[u]nless the court otherwise orders”. In Horizon Resource Management Ltd. v. Blaze Energy Ltd., [2013] A.J. No. 342, 2013 ABCA 139 (Alta. C.A.). the trial judge specifically directed that there would be no Goods and Services Tax (GST) payable on fees. There was no specific direction by the trial judge regarding the payment of GST on disbursements. The order stated that the bills of costs had been assessed and the order allowed the costs as set out in those bills of costs. Horizon’s bill of costs included a claim for GST on disbursements. The Court of PART 10 LAWYERS’ CHARGES, RECOVERABLE COSTS OF LITIGATION, AND SANCTIONS
